title: Groupe de Galois motivique : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, continued from the previous pages of this 1965 letter: G is a reductive Q-group and V = G(R)°/K is the homogeneous complex manifold of Hodge structures obtained by conjugating a base Hodge structure i_0 : U -> G_R, where U is the circle group (in modern terms h_0 : S -> G_R). Γ ⊂ G(Z) is arithmetic, and 𝒱/Γ is the tautological 'modular family' of Hodge structures on V/Γ. The question throughout is which such families are 'motivic', i.e. come from a relative motive over an algebraic V/Γ.

The page states a necessary condition, assuming the Hodge and Tate conjectures. For every g ∈ G(R)° and every finite-index Γ_0 ⊂ G(Z), let H be the smallest algebraic Q-subgroup with two properties: H_R contains g·i_0(U_R)·g^{-1}, the Mumford–Tate datum at the point gK, and H contains Γ_0, the monodromy of a finite cover. The condition is that H = G.

Implicit argument:
- A tensor in the fibre at gK that is a Hodge class there and invariant under the monodromy Γ_0 is algebraic, by the Hodge conjecture.
- A monodromy-invariant algebraic class on one fibre extends to the whole family; this is the global invariant cycle / Tate-type input.
- So the tensor is Hodge at every point, hence fixed by all g'·i_0(U)·g'^{-1}, which generate G.
- Therefore H and G fix the same tensors, so H = G (for reductive H, via Chevalley/Deligne).

In modern language this is the theorem of the fixed part. If a class is monodromy-invariant and Hodge at one point, it is Hodge everywhere. Equivalently, the generic Mumford–Tate group is generated by the algebraic monodromy group together with the Mumford–Tate group of any single fibre; compare André 1992, where monodromy is normal in the derived Mumford–Tate group. Deligne (Hodge II, 1971) proved this unconditionally for geometric families, and Schmid did so for polarizable VHS on quasi-projective bases.

The boxed and struck-out paragraph proposed testing the condition on the usual Siegel space: if it failed there, Hodge or Tate would be false. Grothendieck then asks in the margin whether G(Z) is always Zariski-dense in G when G_R is semisimple without compact factors. That is the Borel density theorem (1960). It makes the condition automatic in that case, since Γ_0 alone is Zariski-dense, so the test is empty. This explains the deletion.

Combined with the previous page, the condition can only bite when G has compact factors. There, for example for V = X compact homogeneous, simply connected, so trivial monodromy, it forces the family to be constant. Grothendieck saw this as a paradox ('I really do not know what to believe'). It is resolved by Griffiths transversality (1968): non-horizontal tautological families on non-Hermitian period domains are not variations of Hodge structure and cannot be geometric.

The final question asks the correspondent (whose 1965 Boulder talk Grothendieck has just read; Mumford's 'Families of abelian varieties' or Kuga's or Satake's Boulder papers are plausible candidates) whether the image of V/Γ in the Siegel modular variety is algebraic, or at least constructible. The answer is yes: by Baily–Borel (1966) and Borel's extension theorem (1972), the image is a closed algebraic subvariety, and these give the Shimura varieties of Hodge type.
errors: The condition is stated with 'smallest algebraic subgroup containing'. The tensor-invariant deduction only gives H = G if H is reductive (or one works with the Tannakian closure); this is a minor gap.

As the marginal question itself reveals, the condition is vacuous when G_R has no compact factors (Borel density 1960), so the proposed Siegel test could not detect anything. The deletion is justified.
The hypotheses 'granting Tate's and Hodge's conjectures' are unnecessary: the conclusion holds unconditionally by Deligne's theorem of the fixed part (1971).

ideas.what: Necessary condition for a modular family of Hodge structures to be motivic: the group generated by the Hodge cocharacter at any one point and the monodromy must be the full group G
ideas.modern_name: Theorem of the fixed part; generic Mumford–Tate group generated by monodromy and the pointwise MT group; monodromy normal in the MT group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Hodge II, 1971); Schmid (1973); André (1992); Mumford's 1966 analysis of Mumford–Tate groups

ideas.what: Is G(Z) Zariski-dense in G when G_R is semisimple without compact factors?

ideas.usually_credited_to: Baily–Borel 1966; Borel extension theorem 1972; Satake; Deligne (Travaux de Shimura 1971)

missed.claim: In 1965 Grothendieck derived, from the Hodge and Tate conjectures, what amounts to the theorem of the fixed part / the monodromy–Mumford–Tate relation. He used it as a criterion for which group-theoretic families of Hodge structures can be motivic, anticipating Deligne's 1971 theorem and the later Shimura-datum axioms. It is a historical priority detail rather than new mathematics.
missed.quote: a necessary condition for V/Γ to be algebraic and the Hodge-structure 𝒱/Γ over V/Γ algebraic too, is (granting Tate's and Hodge's conjectures): ... the smallest alg. subgroup H of G such that H_R contains g[i_0(U_R)]g^{-1} and Γ_0 is G itself.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It documents that the motivic-Galois-group programme already contained, in 1965, the fixed-part / monodromy argument now central to Mumford–Tate domain theory. The paradox it produced for compact G was later resolved by Griffiths transversality. This is of historiographical interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: A clean early formulation of the fixed-part / monodromy–MT-group principle in the context of which homogeneous families are motivic, predating Deligne. However, the mathematics was all later established. The density question is Borel's 1960 theorem, and the algebraicity question was answered by Baily–Borel and Borel.
transcription_corrections: The paragraph 'I did not try to test directly this condition ... conjecture is wrong!' is boxed and struck through with diagonal lines in the image. The marginal 'Question: If G_R is semi-simple without compact factor ... ?!' is written inside the box's lower right and is not struck.
In 'I did not try', the word 'not' appears overwritten or emphasized; the reading 'I did not try' is correct.
'Boulder talk (which I just read)' is correct; the last paragraph is marked by a curly brace in the left margin.
